title: From a convincing image to a defensible conclusion
subtitle: Eight rooms. Six minutes. A different way of looking.

stops.label: Exhibition Foyer
stops.question: Would you trust a restoration just because it looks convincing?
stops.look: Take in the painting and the question on the wall. This museum separates visual plausibility from evidence of a trustworthy restoration.
stops.takeaway: A beautiful result is a starting point, not a verdict.

stops.label: Study Design
stops.question: What makes a comparison fair?
stops.look: Open an experimental path and look at what changes—and what stays controlled. Notice that the portrait review is a linked study, not a replacement for the main experiment.
stops.takeaway: Understand the test before interpreting its result.

stops.label: Metric Framework
stops.question: Can two measurements disagree and both be useful?
stops.look: Try two evidence lenses on the same restoration, then change the inspected region. Read what each measurement can and cannot tell you.
stops.takeaway: Different measurements answer different questions; there is no universal quality score.

stops.label: Model Gallery
stops.question: What changes when the restoration method changes?
stops.look: Open a method’s evidence and compare its capabilities, saved results, and limitations. Keep the experiment and candidate identity in view.
stops.takeaway: A method’s strengths do not make it the winner of every case.

stops.label: Stability Lab
stops.question: Would the conclusion survive a different seed or condition?
stops.look: Inspect one saved stability comparison. Notice which repeated runs or perturbations exist, and where uncertainty evidence is unavailable.
stops.takeaway: Stability evidence is population-specific, not calibrated confidence.

stops.label: Trustworthiness
stops.question: What should make a human reviewer pause?
stops.look: Open a review flag and trace its meaning and evidence. The Focused Portrait Review is an optional side room if you want to look more closely at faces and hands.
stops.takeaway: Review flags guide attention; they are not conservation approval.

stops.label: Case Explorer
stops.question: Can you connect the image, the numbers, and the caution?
stops.look: Compare the clean reference, damaged input, mask, and restoration. Switch an evidence layer, then open a saved measurement or report for that exact candidate.
stops.takeaway: Keep every conclusion attached to the exact painting, case, and candidate.

stops.label: Research Archive
stops.question: Could someone else find the evidence behind your conclusion?
stops.look: Open the final report, trace a source, or inspect a checksum record. Then visit a limitation drawer: what the study cannot claim belongs in the archive too.
stops.takeaway: Traceable evidence—and explicit limits—make a conclusion defensible.

detour.label: Focused Portrait Review
detour.question: What changes when you look closely at faces and hands?
detour.look: This shared side room examines recorded portrait observations. It is an optional detour, outside the six-minute route.

invitations.label: I want to look closely
invitations.text: Begin with one painting. Compare the damage, restoration, and evidence layers.

invitations.label: I’m curious about the methods
invitations.text: Meet the restoration approaches through their saved results and limitations.

invitations.label: Show me the reasons to pause
invitations.text: Read the warning signs and the questions they leave for human review.

invitations.label: Take me to the source
invitations.text: Browse original reports, provenance, and the limits behind the claims.
